paras: The Wellston church whitecapping was a night attack in early October 1903 at Wellston, Oklahoma Territory, in which unidentified parties destroyed the tent of Albert Boyd, a Black man living on lots bought by the town's colored Baptists for a church. The attackers left a notice signed 'Citizens of Wellston' warning that no church for colored people would be allowed and threatening 'sterner measures' if building went on. No one was hurt, and the coverage reports no arrests.

The colored Baptists of Wellston had bought four lots on which to build a church, and Boyd put up a tent there as his residence while the church was prepared. Word of dissatisfaction among some residents reached the Black congregation, and Boyd said he offered to sell the lots if the church was objectionable. Because no one offered to buy, he assumed there was no serious objection and the congregation went ahead.

While Boyd was away from Wellston overnight, the tent was destroyed and his household furniture thrown on the ground. On the spot the attackers posted a typed notice, dated Wellston, O. T., Oct. 8, 1903, declaring that a church for colored people would 'under no consideration be allowed by the citizens of the town of Wellston.' It closed with the warning that 'sterner measures will be adopted when we next call' and was signed 'Citizens of Wellston.' The Chandler report described the notice as the work of an amateur typist, with the body in capitals, the signature in small letters and poor punctuation.

Boyd and other Black residents of Wellston went to Chandler to consult the officers about prosecution. Boyd said he thought he knew who had done it but could not swear to it, and he did not know what further steps his people would take. The county attorney was out of town, and no report of arrests or charges appears in the coverage.

The story reached print through a Chandler paper, which the Wichita Daily Eagle credited as the Publicist and the Guthrie Daily Leader called 'a Chandler exchange.' The Guthrie Daily Leader ran it on October 15 under the headline 'White Caps at Wellston' with the deck 'Citizens Become Enraged and Tear Down a Negro's Tent,' printing the notice in full. The next day the Wichita Daily Eagle carried a fuller Chandler dispatch headed 'Bought Four Lots,' which added Boyd's own statements, the notice's date and the appeal to the Chandler officers. Neither paper commented on the attack, and no coverage in the Black press was found.

The two accounts differ on the night of the attack: the Guthrie Daily Leader placed it on Thursday night, while the Wichita Daily Eagle said Friday night. The notice's date of October 8, 1903, a Thursday, is consistent with the Guthrie version.

bases: An anonymous night party destroyed a Black man's tent and posted a notice signed 'Citizens of Wellston' threatening 'sterner measures' if a Black church was built, and the Guthrie Daily Leader headed the story 'White Caps at Wellston' (A1, A2).
The two reports agree on the core event but both derive from a Chandler paper (A2 credits the Publicist, A1 'a Chandler exchange'), so they are not independent (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Chandler Publicist report (via Chandler dispatch)
accounts.gist: Friday night, while Boyd was out of town, parties destroyed his tent, scattered his furniture and posted a typed notice dated Oct. 8 forbidding a colored church; Boyd sought help from Chandler officers.

accounts.label: Guthrie Daily Leader rewrite of a Chandler exchange
accounts.gist: The same story under a 'White Caps' headline, placing the attack on Thursday night and saying citizens had become dissatisfied with the church.

accounts.label: Albert Boyd
accounts.gist: Boyd said he had offered to sell the lots if the church was objectionable and thought he knew who did it but could not swear to it.

framing.detail: The Guthrie Daily Leader labeled the act whitecapping ('White Caps at Wellston') and said 'Citizens Become Enraged', printing the notice in full without comment.
The Wichita Daily Eagle ran the Chandler dispatch under 'Bought Four Lots', giving Boyd's side and noting the amateur typing of the notice.

conflicts.note: The notice itself is dated Oct. 8, 1903 (A2), which fits Thursday night; both papers rely on the same Chandler source, so neither is clearly better.
